name: iHeartRadio
tagline: Streaming app for live broadcast radio stations, curated music playlists, and a large podcast catalog.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely build a radio and podcast player in an afternoon: audio element, stream URL, play button, done. What you cannot build is the right to stream hundreds of licensed terrestrial stations, the on-demand music catalog that the paid tiers exist for, or the exclusive podcast slate. iHeart is a broadcast company with an app attached, not an app with content attached. The closest honest DIY is a player on top of the open internet radio directories plus podcast RSS, which covers live-radio-and-podcasts listening surprisingly well but drops the on-demand songs, the local personalities you actually wanted, and anything exclusive. Build that if you mostly listen to live streams and shows, pay if you want a specific station's licensed feed or a music library.
coreLoopDIY: A local web player that browses the open Radio Browser station directory, streams stations, subscribes to podcast RSS feeds, and remembers your favorites and playback positions in SQLite.
requirements: Internet connection for public station directories and podcast feeds
A browser that can play MP3/AAC/HLS streams
whatYouLose: Licensed streams for stations that are not publicly redistributable, which is a lot of the ones people want
On-demand music and playlist features from the paid tiers
Polished mobile apps, CarPlay, Android Auto, smart speaker and TV integrations
Offline downloads and cross-device sync of where you left off
moatNotes: Broadcast licensing plus music licensing. Two separate legal regimes, neither available to a hobby project.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly because they want one specific station, show, or host, and the only legal place that feed lives is the app that owns it. The paid tiers add on-demand playback and unlimited skips, which is really a music licensing product bolted onto a radio brand. Nobody is paying for the UI, and the free tier covers most listening anyway, so the real competitor is Spotify rather than your weekend build.
notes: The player is a one-sitting build; the broadcast rights are not. The moat is content licensing: terrestrial station feeds and a music catalog, neither of which you can self-host.
prompt:
Build a local-first internet radio and podcast player called "Tuner". No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Node 20 + Express + TypeScript for the server
- better-sqlite3 for storage, single file data/tuner.db
- Plain server-rendered HTML with htmx for interactions, one CSS file, no React, no build step beyond tsc
- Runs with `npm run dev` on http://localhost:5173

Server responsibilities:
- Proxy and cache calls to the Radio Browser API (https://all.api.radio-browser.info) for station search by name, country, tag, and codec. Cache responses in SQLite for 24 hours, send a descriptive User-Agent.
- Proxy podcast RSS fetches to avoid browser CORS issues, parse feeds with a small XML parser, extract title, description, artwork, and episodes with enclosure URL, duration, and pubDate.
- Proxy audio streams only if the direct URL fails CORS; otherwise let the browser hit the stream directly.

Schema: stations(id, uuid, name, stream_url, favicon, country, tags, favorite, last_played_at), podcasts(id, feed_url, title, artwork, last_checked_at), episodes(id, podcast_id, guid, title, audio_url, duration, pub_date, position_seconds, finished).

UI, three pages:
1. Radio: search box, results grid with station name, country, bitrate, favorite toggle. Click plays.
2. Podcasts: paste a feed URL to subscribe, list of subscriptions, episode list per show with resume-from-position.
3. Favorites: starred stations and in-progress episodes.

A persistent bottom player bar on every page: HTML5 audio element, play/pause, volume, current title, and for podcasts a seek bar plus 15s skip buttons. Write playback position back to SQLite every 10 seconds via a small POST.

Also: import/export favorites and subscriptions as OPML/JSON, a dark theme by default, and graceful handling of dead streams (mark station as failed after two errors, show it dimmed).

Out of scope, do not attempt: on-demand music catalogs, anything requiring licensed or paid station feeds, mobile apps, user accounts, recommendations.

Secrets: none required. If you add an optional Podcast Index API lookup, read keys from .env and degrade silently when absent. Finish with a README covering setup, the legal note that only publicly listed streams are used, and known limitations.
